input:
This passage sets out the inventory policy that has been adopted for a resin grade, focusing in particular on the level of safety stock that should be held. Mean demand is 3027 units per week, with a standard deviation of 874 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 2 weeks. On this basis, the safety stock for a 95% cycle service level has been set at 2039 units, a figure that is designed to ensure that the business is well positioned to maintain continuity of supply in the face of the normal variability that is inevitably present in weekly demand patterns.

It is important to note the assumptions that underpin this policy. Demand is treated as normal, which means that the spread of weekly demand is summarised by the standard deviation and the safety stock scales accordingly, and demand is also treated as independent between weeks, so that the variation experienced over the lead time is the variation of unrelated weekly draws rather than of a sustained run in a single direction. Seasonal peaks, however, are excluded from the policy altogether, which means that the safety stock figure should not be regarded as providing cover for such periods: a seasonal peak that raises weekly demand above the mean for the duration of the lead time will steadily draw the safety stock down and may well exhaust it entirely, and any cover for those periods will need to be determined separately, on the basis of the peak itself, at the appropriate time.

Safety stock for the resin grade is 2039 units, set against a mean demand of 3027 units per week with a standard deviation of 874 units per week and a replenishment lead time of 2 weeks. The figure is the stock held above mean lead-time demand so that demand over the lead time is met from stock at a 95% cycle service level, and a shortage is recorded against a cycle only when lead-time demand runs past the mean and the safety stock together. The figure is reviewed when the demand record changes materially, since both quantities it rests on are properties of that record rather than of the store that holds the stock.

The policy rests on two stated treatments of the demand data. Demand is treated as normal, so the spread of weekly demand is summarised by the standard deviation and the safety stock scales with it; and demand is treated as independent between weeks, so the variation over a two-week lead time is the variation of two unrelated draws rather than of a run in one direction. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy. The stock figure therefore covers ordinary week-to-week variation at the stated service level and does not cover a seasonal peak: a peak that lifts weekly demand above the mean for the length of the lead time draws the safety stock down and can exhaust it, and cover for such periods has to be set by a separate decision on the peak itself.
